title: Statement on Inclusive and Sustainable Artificial Intelligence for People and the Planet
original_title: Déclaration sur une intelligence artificielle inclusive et durable pour les peuples et la planète
issuing_body: Signatories of the AI Action Summit, Paris (hosted by the French Presidency): 63 countries, the African Union Commission and the EU
summary: Statement of the AI Action Summit in Paris that sets six priorities: accessible AI to reduce digital divides; AI that is open, inclusive, transparent, ethical, safe, secure and trustworthy; innovation without market concentration; AI that shapes work and labour markets positively; sustainable AI; and international cooperation on governance. It commends the Bletchley and Seoul summits' work on AI safety and notes the voluntary commitments made there, says the signatories will keep addressing AI risks to information integrity and continue work on AI transparency, and reaffirms the commitment to a UN Global Dialogue on AI governance and an Independent International Scientific Panel on AI.
safety_topics: international cooperation; transparency & labelling
notes: Published on 11 February 2025, the second day of the AI Action Summit, held in Paris on 10 and 11 February 2025. The signatory list names 63 countries, the African Union Commission and the EU; the United States and the United Kingdom are not on it. A footnote limits the statement to civil applications and use of AI. Founding members launched a Public Interest AI Platform and Incubator under it. The International AI Safety Report 2025 (INT-09) was published ahead of the summit.

title: AI Impact Summit Declaration
issuing_body: Participants of the India AI Impact Summit 2026, New Delhi (hosted by the Government of India)
summary: Declaration of the AI Impact Summit in New Delhi, held after the Bletchley, Seoul and Paris summits. It calls for international cooperation along seven pillars: human capital, access for social empowerment, trustworthiness of AI systems, energy efficiency, AI in science, democratising AI resources, and AI for economic growth and social good. Its secure and trusted AI section calls secure, trustworthy and robust AI foundational to trust and recognises security in AI systems, industry-led voluntary measures, technical solutions and policy frameworks across the AI lifecycle. It notes the voluntary Trusted AI Commons, a platform of technical resources, tools, benchmarks and best practices.
safety_topics: international cooperation; evaluation & testing
notes: The declaration is headed 'AI Impact Summit Declaration, New Delhi (February 18 - 19, 2026)', and its preamble says the participants gathered in New Delhi on 19 February 2026; the European Commission announced on 20 February 2026 that the EU would endorse it, and the Australian government gives the summit as 19 and 20 February 2026, so only the month is given. The endorsement list published with the text names 89 endorsers: 87 countries, among them the USA, China, India, Russia and the UK, plus the EU and IFAD. Under its pillars the declaration takes note of voluntary deliverables, among them the Charter for the Democratic Diffusion of AI, the Global AI Impact Commons, the Trusted AI Commons and its guidance note, the International Network of AI for Science Institutions and the Voluntary Guiding Principles on Resilient, Innovative, and Efficient Artificial Intelligence.

title: The Bletchley Declaration by Countries Attending the AI Safety Summit, 1-2 November 2023
issuing_body: Governments attending the AI Safety Summit at Bletchley Park (28 countries and the EU), hosted by the UK Government
summary: Declaration by 28 countries and the EU on the risks of 'frontier' AI: highly capable general-purpose models, and narrow AI with harmful capabilities, that match or exceed today's most advanced models. It warns of substantial risks from intentional misuse or unintended issues of control, names cybersecurity, biotechnology and disinformation, and sees potential for serious, even catastrophic, harm. Its agenda is a shared scientific understanding of these risks and risk-based national policies, with safety testing, evaluations and transparency from developers of frontier AI, and an international network of scientific research on frontier AI safety.
safety_topics: general-purpose / frontier AI; catastrophic risk; evaluation & testing; transparency & labelling; international cooperation; research priorities
notes: Agreed at the AI Safety Summit at Bletchley Park, 1-2 November 2023; the countries represented include the US, China and the EU. New Zealand joined the commitment on 23 October 2024, and GOV.UK updated the publication on 13 February 2025 to include it as a signatory. The participants said they would meet again in 2024. The International AI Safety Report (interim report INT-08, full report INT-09) was launched at this summit. GOV.UK also offers a Latin American Spanish version of the publication.

issuing_body: Leaders of Australia, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, Republic of Korea, Singapore, UK, US and the EU

title: Frontier AI Safety Commitments, AI Seoul Summit 2024
issuing_body: AI organisations that agreed to the commitments (20 by February 2025), announced by the UK and Republic of Korea governments at the AI Seoul Summit; published by the UK Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
summary: Leading AI developers commit to assess frontier-model risks across the lifecycle and to set and monitor thresholds for intolerable severe risks. They also commit to publish a safety framework and report publicly on implementation, with deeper information shared with trusted actors such as home governments.

Magic, Minimax, 01.ai and NVIDIA were added on 7 February 2025, making 20. title: Seoul Ministerial Statement for advancing AI safety, innovation and inclusivity: AI Seoul Summit 2024
issuing_body: Ministers of 27 countries and a representative of the EU (AI Seoul Summit ministerial session)

title: Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence and Human Rights, Democracy and the Rule of Law
issuing_body: Council of Europe Committee of Ministers
summary: A binding treaty under which Parties must ensure that activities within the lifecycle of AI systems are consistent with human rights, democracy and the rule of law. It requires measures on transparency and oversight, including identification of AI-generated content, accountability, equality, privacy, reliability and safe innovation; remedies, procedural safeguards and notice of interacting with an AI system; and a graduated framework to identify, assess and mitigate risks, with testing where appropriate and possible bans or moratoria. It applies to public authorities; for private actors, each Party declares how it addresses risks. National defence is excluded.
safety_topics: accountability & liability; transparency & labelling; human oversight; risk-based classification; public-sector use; international cooperation
notes: Adopted by the Council of Europe Committee of Ministers on 17 May 2024 and opened for signature in Vilnius on 5 September 2024; the English and French texts are equally authentic. Under Article 30 it enters into force on the first day of the month after a three-month period following the date on which five signatories, at least three of them Council of Europe member States, have consented to be bound. The EU signed on 5 September 2024 and approved the Convention by Council Decision (EU) 2026/1080 of 21 April 2026, after the European Parliament's consent of 11 March 2026; the text was published in the EU Official Journal on 13 May 2026 (OJ L, 2026/1081), and the EU declared that it applies the Convention to private actors through the AI Act. EUR-Lex gives the date of entry into force as unknown (pending notification) or not yet in force. Parties need not apply it to activities protecting their national security interests. A Conference of the Parties follows its implementation, and each Party reports to it within two years of becoming a Party.

title: Methodology for the Risk and Impact Assessment of Artificial Intelligence Systems from the Point of View of Human Rights, Democracy and the Rule of Law (HUDERIA Methodology) and HUDERIA Model
issuing_body: Council of Europe Committee on Artificial Intelligence (CAI)
summary: Non-binding Council of Europe guidance for assessing the risks and impacts of AI systems on human rights, democracy and the rule of law across their lifecycle, for public and private actors. The Methodology sets out a context-based risk analysis (COBRA) with scoping, risk factors, impact mapping and triage; a stakeholder engagement process; a risk and impact assessment; and a mitigation plan, with iterative review. The Model's COBRA Resources list risk factors in an AI system's application, design and development, and deployment contexts, and illustrative areas of concern and sectors. Parties to the Framework Convention may use or adapt it; it is not a means of implementing the Convention.
safety_topics: risk-based classification; human oversight; accountability & liability
notes: The CAI adopted the HUDERIA Methodology at its 12th plenary meeting on 26-28 November 2024, and the HUDERIA Model's Context Based Risk Analysis (COBRA) Resources (CAI(2025)6rev2, dated 5 November 2025) at its 14th plenary meeting on 3-5 November 2025; the Commission's note forwarding the Model to the Council gives 6 November 2025 as the date of that adoption. The CAI's work on HUDERIA was to continue in its successor committee, the Steering Committee on New and Emerging Technologies (CDNET).

title: Hiroshima Process International Guiding Principles for Organizations Developing Advanced AI Systems

title: Hiroshima Process International Code of Conduct for Organizations Developing Advanced AI Systems
issuing_body: G7 Leaders (Hiroshima AI Process, Japanese G7 Presidency)
summary: Voluntary code that turns the Guiding Principles into 11 actions for organisations developing advanced AI systems. They call for internal and independent external testing such as red-teaming at several points in the lifecycle, with attention to chemical, biological, radiological and nuclear risks, offensive cyber capabilities, self-replicating models and chain-reaction events; post-deployment monitoring and incident sharing; and public transparency reports. Other actions cover risk management and governance policies, security of model weights and insider threats, content authentication such as watermarking, safety research, international standards and data protection.
safety_topics: general-purpose / frontier AI; evaluation & testing; catastrophic risk; incident reporting; transparency & labelling; deepfakes & synthetic media

title: Hiroshima AI Process Comprehensive Policy Framework (Hiroshima AI Process G7 Digital & Tech Ministers' Statement)
issuing_body: G7 Digital and Tech Ministers; endorsed by G7 Leaders (6 Dec 2023)
summary: Framework endorsed by the G7 Digital and Tech Ministers as the outcome of the Hiroshima AI Process under Japan's 2023 presidency, described as the first successful international framework of guiding principles and a code of conduct for advanced AI. Its four elements are the OECD report towards a G7 common understanding on generative AI, the Guiding Principles extended to all AI actors with a 12th principle on responsible use, digital literacy and sharing information on emerging risks, the Code of Conduct for organisations developing advanced AI systems, and project-based cooperation on content authentication, labelling of AI-generated content and countering disinformation.
safety_topics: general-purpose / frontier AI; transparency & labelling; deepfakes & synthetic media; international cooperation
notes: Agreed at a virtual meeting of the G7 Digital & Tech Ministers on 1 Dec 2023, with a work plan for 2024 under the Italian presidency that includes developing monitoring tools to help organisations stay accountable for applying the Code of Conduct; G7 Leaders endorsed the framework and the work plan in their statement of 6 Dec 2023. The framework states that users of open-sourced advanced AI are not exempt from the relevant principles. Later G7 texts that continue the Hiroshima AI Process include the Italian presidency's ministerial declaration with an annex on advancing its outcomes (15 Mar 2024), the Canadian presidency's industry, digital and technology ministerial declaration (Dec 2025) and the French presidency's ministerial declaration of May 2026 (G7-04). The HAIP Friends Group adopted an action plan in March 2026 (INT-20), and the OECD runs the HAIP Reporting Framework (OECD-02).

title: Action Plan on Cybersecurity and Artificial Intelligence
short_title: EU Action Plan on Cybersecurity and AI
issuing_body: European Commission
summary: A Commission communication on the risks and opportunities of advanced AI for cybersecurity: AI can help detect vulnerabilities and prevent attacks, but it can be misused to automate attacks and find weaknesses at unprecedented speed and scale. To promote the safe use of advanced AI, the Commission will strengthen EU capacity to evaluate AI models before they are placed on the market, in line with the AI Act, with third-party assessment of capabilities and risks that supports the AI Office; define with ENISA a European blueprint for structured access to advanced AI for cybersecurity; and create with ENISA and the JRC a secure platform to test AI for critical sectors.

notes: Adopted at Strasbourg on 7 July 2026 and sent to the Council on 8 July 2026 (Council document 11711/26). The plan has three objectives: promoting the safe and responsible use of advanced AI, reinforcing the EU's cybersecurity and resilience, and scaling up Europe's AI capabilities for cybersecurity; the communication sets them out as three pillars, followed by work with like-minded partners. It promotes the implementation of the NIS2 Directive and the Cyber Resilience Act, encourages organisations to use AI, including open-source models, to find and fix vulnerabilities, and has ENISA provide guidance and a campaign to secure critical open source software. The Commission will launch an EU Grand Challenge on AI for cybersecurity. Its nine key actions include the EU evaluation capacity for AI models (2027), the access Blueprint and the testing platform (Q4 2026), ENISA guidance on protection against AI-powered threats (from Q3 2026), a pilot Critical Open Source Resilience Campaign (Q4 2026), the Grand Challenge (Q4 2026) and training modules for cybersecurity professionals (Q4 2026). The Blueprint will not introduce new obligations for providers, the evaluation capacity will not be a conformity assessment body, and the testing platform is for testing AI for cyber resilience, not for evaluating general-purpose AI models for compliance with the AI Act. The Commission will set up a working group with ENISA, the European Defence Agency and the Member States on the security risks of frontier AI in defence and dual-use critical systems. Internationally, it will work in the G7 and the UN, with the Network of Advanced AI Measurement, Evaluation and Science, and with NATO, and it will regularly assess the plan's implementation. The plan builds on the AI Act, the Cyber Resilience Act, the NIS2 Directive, the Digital Operational Resilience Act and the Cyber Solidarity Act.

title: Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 8 July 2026 amending Regulations (EU) 2024/1689, (EU) 2018/1139 and (EU) 2023/1230 as regards the simplification of the implementation of harmonised rules on artificial intelligence (Digital Omnibus on AI)
issuing_body: European Parliament and Council of the European Union
summary: Amends the AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) to simplify its implementation. It moves the application of the high-risk rules from 2 August 2026 to 2 December 2027 for Annex III systems and 2 August 2028 for systems covered by Annex I product legislation, and adds prohibitions, applying from 2 December 2026, on AI systems that generate non-consensual intimate or sexually explicit material of identifiable people or child sexual abuse material. It makes the AI Office exclusively competent for AI systems built on a provider's own general-purpose AI models and for AI in very large online platforms and search engines, and extends measures for SMEs to small mid-cap enterprises.
safety_topics: risk-based classification; prohibited practices; general-purpose / frontier AI; transparency & labelling; deepfakes & synthetic media; child safety
notes: Commission proposal COM(2025) 836 final of 19 November 2025 (procedure 2025/0359(COD)), part of the digital omnibus package. As proposed, the high-risk rules would have applied 6 months (Annex III) or 12 months (Annex I) after a Commission decision confirming that support measures such as harmonised standards were available, and in any case by 2 December 2027 and 2 August 2028; generative AI systems already on the market would have had until 2 February 2027 to meet the Article 50(2) marking obligation. The adopted text fixes the high-risk dates and sets 2 December 2026 for marking. The European Parliament adopted its position on 16 June 2026 and the Council its decision on 29 June 2026; the act was signed at Strasbourg on 8 July 2026, published in the Official Journal (OJ L, 2026/1744) on 24 July 2026 and entered into force on 27 July 2026, the third day after publication. Dates set by the amendments: the new prohibitions in Article 5(1), points (ba) and (bb), apply from 2 December 2026; providers of generative AI systems placed on the market before 2 August 2026 must meet the Article 50(2) marking obligation by 2 December 2026; each Member State must have at least one national AI regulatory sandbox operational by 2 August 2027; the high-risk rules of Chapter III, Sections 1 to 3, apply from 2 December 2027 for Annex III systems and from 2 August 2028 for Annex I systems. The AI Office's exclusive competence for systems based on general-purpose AI models excludes AI systems related to Annex I products, systems in point 2 of Annex III, systems of law enforcement and border management authorities and financial institutions that fall under Article 74(6), and systems used in the administration of justice. The regulation also simplifies registration in the EU database of systems that providers assess as not high-risk under Article 6(3), allows processing of special categories of personal data for bias detection and correction where strictly necessary, lets the AI Office set up an AI regulatory sandbox at Union level, and extends real-world testing to high-risk systems covered by Annex I legislation. Machinery moves from Section A to Section B of Annex I, and the Commission is to adopt delegated acts adding AI requirements to the Machinery Regulation (EU) 2023/1230, applying by 2 August 2028. It also amends Regulation (EU) 2018/1139 on civil aviation.

summary: Guidance from the Ministry of Science and ICT on the transparency duties of Article 31 of Korea's AI Basic Act: prior notice that a product or service is operated on the basis of high-impact or generative AI (para. 1); marking that outputs were generated by generative AI (para. 2); and notice or marking of deepfakes, defined as virtual sound, image or video outputs hard to distinguish from reality (text excluded), so that users clearly recognise them (para. 3).
